title: Rosette chain stitch
subtitle: A twisted, coral-like border stitch worked between two parallel lines
excerpt: Rosette chain stitch creates a decorative band of overlapping twisted loops that resemble a string of small rosettes. Each stitch passes under the previous loop before re-entering the fabric, building a raised, textured border. It is worked between two parallel lines and is more complex to manage than most chain variants, but produces a very distinctive result.
sourceNotes: Caulfeild & Saward, Dictionary of Needlework (1882); Thérèse de Dillmont, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (1886).

glossaryTerms.definition: The drawn or traced line on the fabric that guides where the stitches go.
The length of thread currently being stitched with, running from the fabric to the needle.

content.text: Rosette chain stitch is a border stitch worked between two
transfer lines
. The
working thread

is looped and twisted so that each new stitch passes under the upper part of the previous loop before the needle enters the lower line. This twisting action builds a raised ridge along the top of the band and a series of curved petals below it, giving the rosette effect.
What you need

items.label: Thread
items.value: Pearl cotton No. 8 or stranded cotton 3 to 4 strands; a smooth thread shows the twist most clearly

items.label: Fabric
items.value: Medium-weight even-weave linen or cotton; the stitch is dense and needs a stable ground

items.label: Needle
items.value: Crewel needle size 7; a slightly blunt tip helps when sliding under the previous loop

items.label: Hoop
items.value: A hoop is essential; the fabric must be taut so the diagonal bite into the lower line stays consistent

content.text: Working the stitch

Draw two parallel lines 5 to 8 mm apart: an upper line and a lower line. Secure the thread and bring the needle up at point A on the upper line, at the right-hand end of the band (this stitch is worked right to left).

Lay the thread in a clockwise loop to the right of A. Insert the needle into the lower line at point B, angling it so it comes up at point C on the lower line, a short distance to the left of B. The thread loop lies over the needle as it passes from B to C.

Before pulling through, slide the needle tip under the thread that runs from A down to the entry at B, passing from right to left under that thread. The needle now has both the lower loop and the upper thread under its tip.
Pull the thread through to the left. A twisted loop locks at C and a small curved petal forms between the two lines. Do not pull too tight or the petal will flatten.

For the next stitch, slide the needle under the upper bar of the loop just formed (the thread running along the upper line) without piercing the fabric, passing from right to left. Then insert into the lower line at D and bring up at E, with the thread looped clockwise as before, and repeat the slide-under step.

Continue to the left. The upper bar of each stitch lies along the upper line; the petals hang between the lines. Finish by taking the needle down through the last loop to hold it, then fasten on the back.
Common mistakes

items.symptom: The twist does not form; it looks like ordinary chain stitch
items.cause: The needle is not sliding under the descending thread from A to B before pulling through.
items.fix: Before every pull-through, check the needle tip is under that upper thread. This slide-under step is what creates the twist. Work slowly until the sequence is automatic.

items.cause: Irregular spacing between B and C, or uneven tension on each pull-through.
items.fix: Mark the lower line with evenly spaced dots before starting. Pull each stitch to the same tension and let the loop settle before moving to the next.

items.symptom: The band drifts away from the upper line
items.cause: Each new stitch is starting from the lower line rather than from a slide under the previous upper bar.
items.fix: From the second stitch onward, always begin by sliding under the bar of the previous loop along the upper line. This is the connection that keeps the ridge aligned.

content.text: Uses and related stitches
Rosette chain shares its looping structure with
chain stitch
but its knotted upper edge is closer in character to
coral stitch
. For a simpler linked chain border
cable chain stitch
is a good starting point before attempting rosette chain.
